es.q: Discuss the key clinical features that help differentiate bacterial vaginosis from vulvovaginal candidiasis.
es.m:
**Answer:**
- **Discharge colour and consistency:** BV – thin, homogeneous, grey‑white; VVC – thick, white, clumpy, “curdy”.
- **Odour:** BV – fishy, often more noticeable after intercourse or menses; VVC – usually no offensive odour.
- **Vulval symptoms:** VVC – prominent itching, soreness, erythema, oedema, fissures; BV – little or no vulval inflammation or itch.
- **pH:** BV – > 4.5; VVC – ≤ 4.5 (usually 3.8–4.5).
- **Microscopy:** BV – clue cells on wet mount; VVC – budding yeast, pseudohyphae on KOH preparation.
es.s: Vaginal Discharge and Vulvovaginal Infections: Clinical Assessment,: Essay quest

es.q: Describe the predisposing factors for vulvovaginal candidiasis.
es.m:
**Answer:**
- **Recent antibiotic use** – disrupts normal lactobacilli, allowing Candida overgrowth.
- **Pregnancy** – hormonal changes increase glycogen and alter immunity.
- **Diabetes mellitus** – higher glucose levels in vaginal secretions promote fungal growth.
- **Immunosuppression** (e.g., HIV, corticosteroid therapy) – reduces host defence against Candida.
- **Local irritants** – douching, perfumed soaps, vaginal deodorants, or lubricants that disturb the normal flora.
- **Retention of foreign bodies** (e.g., forgotten tampon) – creates a moist environment conducive to Candida.
es.s: Vaginal Discharge and Vulvovaginal Infections: Clinical Assessment,: Essay quest

es.q: Describe the management options for esophageal candidiasis in patients living with HIV.
es.m:
- **Exclusion of Local Agents**: There is no therapeutic role for local topical agents when managing esophageal candidiasis.
- **Route of Administration**: Oral or parenteral administration is chosen based on the severity of odynophagia.
- **First-Line Therapy**: Fluconazole remains the primary first-line recommendation for treatment.
- **Alternative Agents**: Echinocandins, voriconazole, and posaconazole serve as alternative options for refractory disease.
- **Treatment Duration**: Standard duration of systemic antifungal treatment ranges from 14 to 21 days.

ai.title: Candida Infections
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Candida spp. are commensal yeasts that become pathogenic when host immunity is impaired. Clinical syndromes range from superficial mucosal disease to life‑threatening invasive candidiasis, especially in HIV, ICU and transplant patients.

sections.p: Candida species are normal flora of skin and mucosa. They cause disease when epithelial barriers are breached or cell‑mediated immunity is weakened. In low‑resource settings, HIV, malnutrition, malabsorption and prolonged antibiotic use are common predisposing factors.
b: Most common species: C. albicans; others: C. glabrata, C. tropicalis, C. krusei, C. parapsilosis

sections.p: Candida is a budding yeast that forms pseudohyphae and true hyphae when invasive. It adheres to epithelial cells via adhesins and secretes enzymes that degrade host tissues.
b: Pseudohyphae: elongated budding cells; hyphae: true filamentous growth

sections.p: Transmission is mainly endogenous; spores are shed in feces and can contaminate hands. Invasive disease occurs when the organism breaches mucosal surfaces or enters the bloodstream.
b: No airborne spread

sections.p: Superficial disease: oral thrush, esophageal candidiasis, vulvovaginal candidiasis, cutaneous intertrigo. Invasive disease: candidemia, deep organ abscesses, endocarditis.
b: Oral thrush: white plaques on tongue, scrape‑off leaving erythema

sections.p: Clinical assessment plus simple tests. In low‑resource settings, microscopy and culture may be limited; use bedside criteria and empirical treatment when suspicion is high.
b: Oral thrush: visual inspection

t.b: Confirm yeast and pseudohyphae – positive indicates Candida infection
Detects candidemia; a positive result confirms invasive disease and guides therapy
Elevated levels suggest invasive candidiasis; useful when cultures are negative

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first (e.g., stop antibiotics, improve nutrition). Use antifungals with good tissue penetration and low toxicity. Avoid drugs with significant drug‑drug interactions.
b: Fluconazole for superficial disease; echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin) for candidemia

t.b: Treats oral, esophageal and vaginal candidiasis; resistance uncommon in low‑resource settings
First line for candidemia; minimal hepatic metabolism, safe in renal impairment

sections.p: Remember that Candida is an opportunistic pathogen, not a common community spread infection. In HIV patients, oral thrush is a marker of advanced immunosuppression. Invasive candidiasis presents with fever, chills and organ dysfunction; blood cultures are essential.
b: Look for red flags: persistent fever >48h, neutropenia, central lines

sections.p: Candidiasis can mimic bacterial vaginosis, herpes simplex, and bacterial pharyngitis. Distinguish by clinical features and simple tests.
b: Bacterial vaginosis: fishy odor, gray discharge; Candida: cottage‑cheese discharge, pruritus

sections.p: Blood cultures may be negative early; BDG can be falsely elevated in patients with hemodialysis or recent surgery.
b: False negatives in early candidemia

sections.p: If candidemia is suspected, start empiric echinocandin immediately, remove central lines, and monitor organ function.
b: Do not delay until culture results

whenToSeekHelp: Unexplained fever >48h with neutropenia or central line, sudden worsening of oral lesions, signs of sepsis, or organ dysfunction

faq.q: Why is Candida not a common airborne infection?
faq.a: It is a commensal yeast; transmission is mainly endogenous or via contact, not aerosol.

faq.q: What is the first line treatment for oral thrush in a patient with HIV?
faq.a: Fluconazole orally; alternative is nystatin suspension if fluconazole resistance suspected.

faq.q: When should I order a blood culture for suspected candidemia?
faq.a: When the patient has persistent fever >48h, neutropenia, central venous catheter, or unexplained organ dysfunction.

exam: A 32‑year‑old HIV patient presents with painful swallowing and white plaques on the tongue. What is the most appropriate next step? — Confirm diagnosis with scrapings; start fluconazole if no contraindications.

A 45‑year‑old neutropenic patient develops fever and chills. Blood cultures are pending. What empiric therapy should you start? — Initiate an echinocandin (e.g., caspofungin) and remove any central lines.
A woman with vulvovaginal discharge reports itching. Gram stain shows no bacteria. What is the likely diagnosis and treatment? — Candida vulvovaginitis; treat with fluconazole or nystatin.

A patient on broad‑spectrum antibiotics develops a red, moist rash in the groin. What is the differential and first test? — Intertriginous candidiasis; examine for white plaques and consider a KOH prep.
Why is fluconazole avoided in patients with severe hepatic impairment? — It is metabolised hepatically; use echinocandins instead.
A child with persistent diarrhoea and weight loss has oral thrush. What does this indicate? — Advanced immunosuppression; evaluate for HIV and start antiretroviral therapy.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Focused history and a step‑by‑step exam allow rapid differentiation of superficial versus invasive candidiasis and identification of predisposing factors in low‑resource settings.
b: Ask about recent broad‑spectrum antibiotics, corticosteroids, chemotherapy or immunosuppressants.
Inquire about diabetes control, HIV status, pregnancy, malnutrition or recent mucosal trauma (dentures, oral thrush).
Determine presence of indwelling devices (central lines, urinary catheters) or recent surgery.
Ask about fever pattern, chills, dysphagia, odynophagia, chest pain or respiratory symptoms for invasive disease.
Ask about genital itching, discharge character, recent intercourse or douching for vulvovaginal disease.

t.b: Is there white, removable plaque with erythematous base? Positive indicates oral thrush; cannot distinguish Candida species.
Does scraping reveal a raw, bleeding surface? Positive supports candidal infection; cannot rule out bacterial superinfection.
Is there pseudohyphae or budding yeast on KOH prep? Positive confirms candidal vaginitis; negative does not exclude early infection.
Is there macerated, erythematous rash with satellite papules? Positive suggests candidal intertrigo; cannot assess depth of invasion.
Are there chorioretinal lesions? Positive may indicate disseminated candidiasis; absence does not exclude it.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use a tiered approach: bedside microscopy, simple culture, then targeted antigen or molecular tests when available. Interpret each in context of local prevalence and patient factors.
b: Direct microscopy (KOH or Gram stain) answers presence of yeast forms; budding yeasts = Candida, pseudohyphae suggest invasive potential.
Culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar confirms species; growth >48 h indicates infection; colony morphology helps differentiate non‑albicans species.
Blood culture (aerobic and anaerobic bottles) answers candidemia; ≥1 positive bottle = true infection; consider contamination if only one bottle positive.
Serum (1→3)-β‑D‑glucan (BDG) answers systemic fungal burden; >80 pg/mL is positive; false‑positive in hemodialysis, IVIG, bacterial sepsis.
Mannan antigen ELISA answers circulating Candida antigen; >0.125 ng/mL (assay‑specific) is positive; false‑negative early in disease.
PCR for Candida DNA (if available) answers species identification; detection of C. albicans or non‑albicans guides therapy.
Complete blood count with differential answers neutropenia; ANC <500 cells/µL increases invasive risk.
Liver function tests answer drug safety; elevated transaminases may require fluconazole dose adjustment.

t.b: Detects yeast buds/pseudohyphae; positive = candidal thrush; cannot quantify load.

t.a: Sabouraud agar culture of vaginal swab
t.b: Identifies species; growth of C. glabrata suggests fluconazole resistance; no growth after 72 h argues against infection.
Detects candidemia; ≥1 bottle positive = true infection; negative does not rule out early candidemia.
Screen for invasive candidiasis; >80 pg/mL positive; if unavailable, rely on clinical risk and cultures.
Positive when >0.125 ng/mL; supports systemic infection; if unavailable, use BDG or repeat cultures.

t.a: PCR for Candida spp. from blood
t.b: Provides rapid species ID; useful for targeted therapy; if unavailable, start empiric echinocandin.

sections.p: Classification combines clinical syndrome, microbiology and host risk to guide therapy intensity and need for escalation.
b: Superficial mucosal disease: oral thrush, esophageal candidiasis, vulvovaginal candidiasis, cutaneous intertrigo – diagnosed by clinical signs plus microscopy/culture.
Invasive candidiasis: candidemia or deep‑organ infection – requires positive blood culture or tissue biopsy plus compatible clinical picture.
Disseminated candidiasis: ≥2 non‑contiguous organ sites (e.g., liver, spleen, kidney) with microbiologic proof.
Severity scoring (e.g., modified APACHE II for ICU patients) – high score (>15) prompts early echinocandin.
Neutropenic host (ANC <500) or ICU admission automatically classifies infection as severe, requiring systemic therapy.
Pregnancy or severe hepatic impairment modifies drug choice but does not change diagnostic criteria.

sections.p: Several common genital or oral lesions mimic candidiasis; systematic comparison prevents misdiagnosis.
b: Bacterial vaginosis – thin gray discharge, fishy odor, clue cells on wet mount; no pseudohyphae on KOH.
Herpes simplex genital infection – painful vesicles that ulcerate, no yeast on microscopy; Tzanck smear shows multinucleated cells.
Oral leukoplakia – white plaques that do not scrape off, no yeast on KOH; risk factors: tobacco, alcohol.
Oral hairy leukoplakia (EBV) – white corrugated plaques on lateral tongue, HIV association, no yeast on KOH.
Intertriginous psoriasis – well‑demarcated erythema with silvery scale, negative KOH, responds to steroids not antifungals.

t.b: Clue cells, pH >4.5, fishy odor; absence of yeast distinguishes from candidal vaginitis.
Clustered vesicles, positive PCR for HSV; KOH negative for yeast.
Non‑scrapable plaque, negative KOH; risk factors differ.
Corrugated white plaques, EBV PCR positive, KOH negative.
Silvery scale, Auspitz sign, KOH negative; improves with steroids.

sections.p: A structured ladder guides clinicians from immediate stabilisation to definitive antifungal therapy, monitoring, and escalation, with clear drug class choices and contraindications.
b: 1. Assess airway, breathing, circulation; treat sepsis with fluids and broad‑spectrum antibiotics while awaiting cultures.
2. Identify risk level: superficial only → topical azole; mucosal or early invasive → oral fluconazole (if hepatic function permits); severe invasive or candidemia → echinocandin.
3. Remove removable sources of Candida (central venous catheters, contaminated dentures, broad‑spectrum antibiotics).

4. Initiate definitive therapy: echinocandin for candidemia or deep organ involvement; fluconazole for susceptible mucosal disease; consider amphotericin B deoxycholate only if other agents unavailable or resistant.
5. Monitor clinical response (fever curve, lesion size, organ function) and laboratory markers (repeat blood cultures at 48 h, (1→3)‑β‑D‑glucan if available).
6. Escalate if no improvement by 72 h, if cultures remain positive, or if organ dysfunction worsens: switch to a different class (e.g., amphotericin B or higher‑dose echinocandin).
7. Refer to higher‑level care for persistent fungemia, end‑organ involvement (endophthalmitis, meningitis), or when renal/hepatic failure limits drug options.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key adverse effects, drug‑drug interactions and practical steps to mitigate them for the main antifungal classes used in low‑resource settings.
b: Fluconazole: hepatotoxicity (monitor transaminases, avoid in severe hepatic failure), QT prolongation (avoid with other QT‑prolonging drugs, correct electrolytes).
Echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin): mild hepatic enzyme rise; no dose adjustment needed in renal failure; watch for infusion‑related histamine reactions.
Amphotericin B deoxycholate: nephrotoxicity (monitor creatinine, replace potassium and magnesium), infusion‑related fever/chills (premedicate with acetaminophen and antihistamine).
Azole topical agents: local irritation; rare systemic absorption—no routine monitoring needed.
Avoid concomitant strong CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., rifampicin) with fluconazole as they reduce azole levels; adjust azole dose if given with warfarin (increase INR monitoring).

sections.p: Complications of candidiasis and clinical triggers that mandate a higher level of care or change in therapy.
b: Persistent fever >48 h despite appropriate antifungal → consider resistant strain, source control failure, or deep‑seated infection.
Positive blood cultures after 48 h of therapy → switch class or add combination therapy.
New organ dysfunction (renal, hepatic, respiratory) → assess drug toxicity versus disease progression; consider amphotericin B if echinocandin failure.
End‑organ involvement (endophthalmitis, meningitis, osteomyelitis) → require prolonged therapy, possible intravitreal or intrathecal drug delivery, and specialist referral.
Severe electrolyte loss (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia) with amphotericin B → replace electrolytes aggressively; consider switching to echinocandin if feasible.

sections.p: Patient‑specific conditions that alter presentation, diagnostic accuracy, or therapeutic choices for Candida infections.
b: HIV: CD4 < 200 cells/µL predisposes to esophageal and oropharyngeal disease; oral thrush may indicate advanced immunosuppression.
TB co‑infection: rifampicin induces CYP enzymes, lowering azole levels; use echinocandin or adjust azole dose.
Malnutrition: impairs mucosal barrier, increases susceptibility; may blunt inflammatory signs, requiring lower threshold for investigation.
Pregnancy: fluconazole contraindicated, especially first trimester; prefer topical azoles for vulvovaginal disease, echinocandin for invasive disease if benefits outweigh risks.
Diabetes mellitus: hyperglycaemia promotes yeast growth; optimise glucose control to aid clearance.
Herbal remedies (e.g., St. John’s wort) induce CYP3A4 → reduce azole exposure; counsel patients to discontinue.
Alcohol excess: worsens hepatic dysfunction, affecting fluconazole metabolism; monitor liver enzymes.
Renal failure: amphotericin B accumulates, increase nephrotoxicity; prefer echinocandin which is not renally cleared.
Severe hepatic impairment (Child‑Pugh C): fluconazole dose reduction required; echinocandin preferred.

sections.p: Tailored considerations for children, pregnant women, the elderly, people living with HIV and settings with limited laboratory capacity.
b: Children: candidemia incidence high in neonates; use echinocandin as first line; fluconazole dosing requires weight‑based adjustment; avoid amphotericin B deoxycholate if possible due to nephrotoxicity.
Pregnancy: avoid systemic azoles; treat vulvovaginal disease with clotrimazole or miconazole creams; for invasive disease, use echinocandin after risk‑benefit discussion.
Elderly: polypharmacy raises interaction risk; monitor QT interval with fluoroquinolones plus fluconazole; adjust for reduced hepatic reserve.

People with HIV: screen for CD4 count; treat esophageal candidiasis with high‑dose fluconazole (if hepatic function allows) or echinocandin for refractory disease; initiate antiretroviral therapy after acute infection control.

Low‑resource settings: when cultures unavailable, rely on microscopy (pseudohyphae in KOH prep) and clinical response; use topical azoles for mucosal disease, echinocandin if injectable formulation is accessible, otherwise amphotericin B deoxycholate with careful electrolyte monitoring.

facts: Candida albicans forms true hyphae and pseudohyphae; hyphae are required for tissue invasion.
Positive (1,3)-β‑D‑glucan assay: >80 pg/mL suggests invasive candidiasis, but false‑positives occur with haemodialysis or certain antibiotics.
Mannan antigen ELISA: positive when >0.125 ng/mL (cut‑off varies by manufacturer).
Fluconazole is contraindicated in pregnancy, especially first trimester, per WHO guidelines.
Echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin) are first‑line for candidemia and invasive disease.
Th17‑derived IL‑17 and IL‑22 are critical for mucosal Candida defence; deficiency predisposes to chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.
Transition from yeast to hyphal form is triggered by serum, temperature 37 °C, and pH > 7, enhancing endothelial adhesion.
Blood culture sensitivity for candidemia is ~50 %; negative early cultures do not exclude disease.

vivas.q: Define invasive candidiasis and list the two major pathogenic forms of Candida albicans.
vivas.a: Invasive candidiasis is infection of sterile sites (blood, organs) by Candida; the organism can exist as budding yeast and as true hyphae/pseudohyphae, the latter enabling tissue invasion.

vivas.q: What bedside history questions help identify risk for systemic candidiasis?
vivas.a: Ask about recent broad‑spectrum antibiotics, central venous catheters, neutropenia, ICU stay, total parenteral nutrition, and mucosal barrier disruption.

vivas.q: Describe the step‑by‑step oral examination for thrush and what a positive finding looks like.
vivas.a: Inspect tongue for white plaques; gently scrape with tongue depressor—plaques lift leaving erythematous base; absence of pain on scraping suggests Candida.

vivas.q: Interpret a (1,3)-β‑D‑glucan result of 120 pg/mL in a neutropenic patient with fever.
vivas.a: Result exceeds the >80 pg/mL cut‑off, supporting invasive candidiasis; however, consider possible false‑positives and correlate clinically.

vivas.q: Why is fluconazole avoided in the first trimester of pregnancy?
vivas.a: It crosses the placenta and is teratogenic; WHO classifies it contraindicated for vaginal candidiasis in pregnancy.

vivas.q: Explain the mechanism of resistance to fluconazole in Candida species.
vivas.a: Mutations in ERG11 (lanosterol 14‑α‑demethylase) reduce drug binding; overexpression of efflux pumps (CDR1/2, MDR1) also contributes.

vivas.q: A patient with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis has a defect in which cytokine‑producing T‑cell subset?
vivas.a: Deficiency of Th17 cells producing IL‑17 and IL‑22 underlies persistent mucosal infection.

vivas.q: Which structural transition of C. albicans enhances endothelial invasion?
vivas.a: Yeast‑to‑hyphae conversion allows expression of invasins (Als3, Hwp1) that bind endothelial cadherins.

vivas.q: What drug class binds ergosterol and creates pores in the fungal membrane?
What adverse effect of fluconazole is explained by its inhibition of cytochrome P450 in the eye?
vivas.a: Visual disturbances (blurred vision, colour changes) due to retinal photoreceptor toxicity.

vivas.q: How do you differentiate bacterial vaginosis from vulvovaginal candidiasis on exam?
vivas.a: BV: thin grey discharge, fishy odor, clue cells on microscopy; Candida: thick white “cottage‑cheese” discharge, intense pruritus, pseudohyphae on KOH.

vivas.q: List three predisposing factors for vulvovaginal candidiasis.
vivas.a: Antibiotic use, uncontrolled diabetes, and high estrogen states (pregnancy, OCPs).

vivas.q: What is the first step when candidemia is suspected in a patient with a central line?
vivas.a: Draw blood cultures from separate lumens, start empiric echinocandin, and remove the central line promptly.

vivas.q: Why can (1,3)-β‑D‑glucan be falsely elevated in patients on haemodialysis?
vivas.a: Dialysis membranes release glucan fragments that cross‑react with the assay.

vivas.q: Explain why echinocandins are preferred over fluconazole in severe hepatic impairment.
vivas.a: Echinocandins are not hepatically metabolised and require no dose adjustment, whereas fluconazole needs caution and dose reduction.

vivas.q: What bedside test cannot differentiate colonisation from invasive candidiasis?
vivas.a: Direct microscopy of skin scrapings; it shows yeast but does not indicate systemic invasion.

vivas.q: In a low‑resource setting lacking culture, what is the best initial test for oral thrush?
vivas.a: KOH wet mount of oral scrapings; rapid identification of pseudohyphae and yeast.

mcqs.q: A 55‑year‑old ICU patient on total parenteral nutrition develops fever. Blood cultures are pending. Which empiric antifungal is recommended?
mcqs.e: Echinocandins (caspofungin) are first‑line for suspected candidemia in critically ill patients.

mcqs.q: Which cytokine deficiency explains chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis?
mcqs.e: IL‑17 from Th17 cells is essential for mucosal Candida defence.

mcqs.q: A man with HIV presents with dysphagia and white plaques. Endoscopy shows ulcerated lesions. Which drug is most appropriate?
mcqs.e: Fluconazole is first‑line for esophageal candidiasis in HIV.

mcqs.q: Which laboratory finding is most specific for invasive candidiasis?
mcqs.e: Blood culture directly isolates Candida, confirming invasive disease.

mcqs.q: A pregnant woman in her first trimester has vulvovaginal itching and thick discharge. Which treatment is safest?
mcqs.e: Topical azoles are safe in pregnancy; oral fluconazole is contraindicated.

mcqs.q: Resistance to fluconazole most commonly involves mutation of which enzyme?
mcqs.e: ERG11 mutations reduce azole binding, the primary mechanism of fluconazole resistance.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical risk factor for invasive candidiasis?
mcqs.e: Smoking is not a recognized independent risk factor for invasive candidiasis.

mcqs.q: What is the main advantage of using amphotericin B lipid formulations over conventional amphotericin B?
mcqs.e: Lipid formulations markedly lower renal toxicity while retaining efficacy.

cases.v: A 38‑year‑old woman with poorly controlled diabetes presents with a 2‑week history of painful, erythematous intertriginous rash in the groin. KOH prep shows pseudohyphae.

qs.q: What is the most appropriate first‑line therapy?
qs.a: Topical azole (e.g., clotrimazole 1% cream) applied twice daily for 2 weeks.

qs.q: Which additional measure will reduce recurrence?
qs.a: Improve glycaemic control and keep the area dry; use absorbent powder after cleaning.

qs.q: If the rash fails to improve after 2 weeks, what is the next step?
qs.a: Obtain fungal culture and consider systemic fluconazole, after confirming no pregnancy.

cases.v: A 62‑year‑old man in the oncology ward, neutropenic (ANC 400), has persistent fever despite broad‑spectrum antibiotics. Blood cultures are negative after 48 h. (1,3)-β‑D‑glucan is 150 pg/mL.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: Invasive candidemia despite negative cultures, supported by elevated β‑D‑glucan.

qs.q: What empiric antifungal should be started?
What infection control action is essential?
qs.a: Remove any central venous catheter and replace it under sterile conditions.

mistakes: Prescribing oral fluconazole in the first trimester of pregnancy without considering contraindication.
Relying solely on a negative blood culture to rule out candidemia in a neutropenic patient.
Confusing the mannan ELISA cut‑off of >0.125 ng/mL with >0.5 ng/mL, leading to false‑negative interpretation.
Using fluconazole without dose adjustment in severe hepatic failure, ignoring the need for caution.
Failing to remove a central line when candidemia is suspected, prolonging source of infection.
Assuming a positive β‑D‑glucan always indicates candidiasis without accounting for haemodialysis‑related false positives.
Treating vulvovaginal candidiasis with systemic azoles in pregnancy when topical therapy would suffice.
Neglecting to assess for Th17 deficiency in patients with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, missing underlying immunodeficiency.
exam: Define invasive candidiasis and list the two major pathogenic forms of Candida albicans. — Invasive candidiasis is infection of sterile sites (blood, organs) by Candida; the organism can exist as budding yeast and as true hyphae/pseudohyphae, the latter enabling tissue invasion.

What bedside history questions help identify risk for systemic candidiasis? — Ask about recent broad‑spectrum antibiotics, central venous catheters, neutropenia, ICU stay, total parenteral nutrition, and mucosal barrier disruption.

Describe the step‑by‑step oral examination for thrush and what a positive finding looks like. — Inspect tongue for white plaques; gently scrape with tongue depressor—plaques lift leaving erythematous base; absence of pain on scraping suggests Candida.

Interpret a (1,3)-β‑D‑glucan result of 120 pg/mL in a neutropenic patient with fever. — Result exceeds the >80 pg/mL cut‑off, supporting invasive candidiasis; however, consider possible false‑positives and correlate clinically.
Why is fluconazole avoided in the first trimester of pregnancy? — It crosses the placenta and is teratogenic; WHO classifies it contraindicated for vaginal candidiasis in pregnancy.

Explain the mechanism of resistance to fluconazole in Candida species. — Mutations in ERG11 (lanosterol 14‑α‑demethylase) reduce drug binding; overexpression of efflux pumps (CDR1/2, MDR1) also contributes.
A patient with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis has a defect in which cytokine‑producing T‑cell subset? — Deficiency of Th17 cells producing IL‑17 and IL‑22 underlies persistent mucosal infection.
Which structural transition of C. albicans enhances endothelial invasion? — Yeast‑to‑hyphae conversion allows expression of invasins (Als3, Hwp1) that bind endothelial cadherins.
What drug class binds ergosterol and creates pores in the fungal membrane? — Polyenes, exemplified by amphotericin B.
What adverse effect of fluconazole is explained by its inhibition of cytochrome P450 in the eye? — Visual disturbances (blurred vision, colour changes) due to retinal photoreceptor toxicity.

How do you differentiate bacterial vaginosis from vulvovaginal candidiasis on exam? — BV: thin grey discharge, fishy odor, clue cells on microscopy; Candida: thick white “cottage‑cheese” discharge, intense pruritus, pseudohyphae on KOH.
List three predisposing factors for vulvovaginal candidiasis. — Antibiotic use, uncontrolled diabetes, and high estrogen states (pregnancy, OCPs).
What is the first step when candidemia is suspected in a patient with a central line? — Draw blood cultures from separate lumens, start empiric echinocandin, and remove the central line promptly.
Why can (1,3)-β‑D‑glucan be falsely elevated in patients on haemodialysis? — Dialysis membranes release glucan fragments that cross‑react with the assay.
